name: Grey zone lymphoma
aliases: B-cell lymphoma unclassifiable with features intermediate between DLBCL and classic Hodgkin lymphoma

clinicalPearls: A B-cell lymphoma with overlapping morphological and immunophenotypic features that sit between primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma and classic Hodgkin lymphoma
Most cases present as a bulky anterior mediastinal mass in young adults, with a slight male predominance in the mediastinal form

The hallmark is a discordance between morphology and immunophenotype, for example Hodgkin-like cells that strongly retain the B-cell programme including CD20, or large-cell morphology with variable CD15 and CD30
It shares molecular features with both parent entities, including 9p24 alterations affecting JAK2 and the programmed death-ligands
Accurate diagnosis requires an adequate biopsy and expert haematopathology review because of the transitional features
Treatment generally follows an aggressive B-cell lymphoma approach with intensive chemoimmunotherapy rather than a Hodgkin-directed regimen
Outcomes are generally less favourable than either primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma or classic Hodgkin lymphoma treated appropriately
reference.pathophysiology: Grey zone lymphoma occupies a biological continuum between primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma and classic Hodgkin lymphoma, and most cases are thought to derive from a thymic B cell. The tumour cells show a mismatch between appearance and antigen expression, so that cells resembling Reed-Sternberg cells may strongly express B-cell markers, or large pleomorphic cells may variably express the Hodgkin-associated antigens CD15 and CD30. It shares recurrent genetic events with both related entities, particularly amplification of the 9p24 locus that upregulates JAK-STAT signalling and PD-L1/PD-L2, promoting proliferation and immune evasion. This transitional biology explains both the diagnostic difficulty and the intermediate, often more resistant, clinical behaviour.
additionalDifferentials: Classic Hodgkin lymphoma, nodular sclerosis type
additionalInvestigations: Adequate core or excisional biopsy with expert haematopathology review
Extended immunohistochemistry panel including CD20, CD15, CD30, PAX5, CD45 and transcription factors
PET-CT for staging and response assessment of the mediastinal mass
Molecular or FISH studies for 9p24 abnormalities where available
Blood counts, lactate dehydrogenase and organ function before intensive therapy
Assessment for superior vena cava obstruction and airway compromise
redFlags: Superior vena cava obstruction or airway compromise from a bulky mediastinal mass
Rapid clinical deterioration with a large or discordant mass
Pericardial or pleural effusion causing haemodynamic compromise
Discordant biopsy findings between disease sites requiring re-evaluation
reference.prognosis: Grey zone lymphoma generally behaves more aggressively and responds less predictably than either primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma or classic Hodgkin lymphoma, so outcomes tend to be poorer; intensive B-cell-directed chemoimmunotherapy offers the best chance of durable remission and checkpoint inhibition may help in the relapsed setting.
pitfalls: Forcing the tumour into a Hodgkin or diffuse large B-cell category and choosing an inappropriate regimen
Relying on limited immunostaining rather than an extended panel to capture the discordant phenotype
Obtaining inadequate tissue given the mediastinal fibrosis and diagnostic subtlety
Overlooking the young age and bulky mediastinal presentation that should prompt the diagnosis
Assuming a favourable Hodgkin-like outcome despite the more resistant biology
references: British Society for Haematology guidance on aggressive B-cell lymphomas
management: Treat with intensive anti-CD20-based chemoimmunotherapy following an aggressive B-cell lymphoma approach such as dose-adjusted rituximab-EPOCH rather than a Hodgkin-directed regimen
Consider consolidative radiotherapy to residual bulky mediastinal disease
For relapsed or refractory disease, use salvage chemotherapy with autologous stem cell transplantation, and exploit the 9p24 biology with PD-1 checkpoint inhibitors
Manage presenting emergencies including superior vena cava obstruction and airway compromise, with tumour lysis prophylaxis before treatment
Stage and assess response with PET-CT
Secure diagnosis on an adequate core or excisional biopsy with expert haematopathology review given the transitional features
Provide supportive care with antimicrobial prophylaxis and growth factor support during myelosuppression, within a haemato-oncology multidisciplinary team
